prompt: How many axial positions does chair cyclohexane have?
explanation: Chair cyclohexane has six axial positions, parallel to the ring axis, and six equatorial positions, around the ring equator (Figure 4.6.1).

prompt: In chair cyclohexane, how are axial and equatorial positions oriented?

choices.text: Axial positions are parallel to the ring axis; equatorial positions lie in the rough plane of the ring, around its equator
Equatorial positions are parallel to the ring axis; axial positions lie around the ring equator
choices.why: That swaps the two. "Axial" goes with the axis and "equatorial" with the equator.

choices.text: Axial positions all point up and equatorial positions all point down
choices.why: Axial positions alternate between the top and bottom faces from one carbon to the next, and so do equatorial ones.

choices.text: Axial positions are on the carbons in the plane; equatorial positions are on the two end carbons
choices.why: Every carbon has one axial and one equatorial position; the terms describe directions, not which carbons.

explanation: The six axial positions are parallel to the ring axis, while the six equatorial positions are in the rough plane of the ring, around the ring equator (Figure 4.6.1).

prompt: How are the 12 hydrogens of chair cyclohexane distributed among its carbons?

choices.text: Each carbon has one axial and one equatorial hydrogen
Three carbons have two axial hydrogens and three have two equatorial hydrogens
choices.why: A carbon's two positions are always one of each kind. What alternates around the ring is which face each points toward.

choices.text: Each carbon has two axial hydrogens
choices.why: There are only six axial positions in all, one per carbon; the other six are equatorial.

choices.text: It varies, depending on how the chair is drawn
choices.why: Every carbon in chair cyclohexane has exactly one axial and one equatorial position (Figure 4.6.2).

explanation: Each carbon atom in chair cyclohexane has one axial and one equatorial hydrogen, giving six of each in total (Figures 4.6.1 and 4.6.2).

prompt: How many axial hydrogens are on one side (face) of a chair cyclohexane ring?
explanation: Each side of the ring has three axial and three equatorial hydrogens in an alternating arrangement. The other three axial hydrogens are on the opposite face.

prompt: If the top side of a chair cyclohexane has axial hydrogens on carbons 1, 3, and 5, which carbons have equatorial hydrogens on the top side?

choices.text: Carbons 2, 4, and 6
Carbons 1, 3, and 5
choices.why: The equatorial hydrogens of carbons 1, 3, and 5 are on the bottom side. Each face alternates axial and equatorial around the ring.

choices.text: Carbons 1, 2, and 3
choices.why: Positions on a face alternate from one carbon to the next, so they don't come in a run of three neighbors.

choices.text: None; the top side has only axial hydrogens
choices.why: Each side of the ring has three axial and three equatorial hydrogens.

explanation: Each side of the ring has three axial and three equatorial hydrogens in an alternating arrangement. If the top side has axial hydrogens on carbons 1, 3, and 5, it has equatorial hydrogens on carbons 2, 4, and 6 (Figure 4.6.2).

prompt: The top side of a chair cyclohexane has axial hydrogens on carbons 1, 3, and 5. What does the bottom side have on carbons 1, 3, and 5?

choices.text: Equatorial hydrogens
Axial hydrogens
choices.why: Each carbon has only one axial position. Since the axial hydrogens of carbons 1, 3, and 5 point to the top, their bottom-side hydrogens are equatorial.

choices.text: No hydrogens
choices.why: Every carbon has two hydrogens, one axial and one equatorial; for carbons 1, 3, and 5 the bottom-side one is equatorial.

choices.text: One axial and one equatorial hydrogen each
choices.why: Each carbon has one hydrogen on each side, not two on the same side.

explanation: The reverse of the top side is true for the bottom side: carbons 1, 3, and 5 have equatorial hydrogens, while carbons 2, 4, and 6 have axial hydrogens (Figure 4.6.2).

prompt: When are two hydrogens on a chair cyclohexane ring cis to each other?

choices.text: Whenever they are on the same side of the ring, regardless of axial or equatorial, and regardless of whether they're adjacent
Only when both are axial
choices.why: Cis and trans depend only on which side of the ring a group is on, not on whether it is axial or equatorial.

choices.text: Only when they are on adjacent carbons and both equatorial
choices.why: Two hydrogens on the same side are cis whether or not they're adjacent, and whether they're axial or equatorial.

choices.text: Only when one is axial and the other equatorial
choices.why: Axial and equatorial describe direction relative to the ring axis; cis means only that both are on the same side.

explanation: Two hydrogens on the same side of the ring are always cis, regardless of whether they're axial or equatorial and regardless of whether they're adjacent. Two hydrogens on opposite sides are always trans.

prompt: In chair cyclohexane, what is the relationship between the axial hydrogen on carbon 1 and the axial hydrogen on carbon 2?

choices.text: Trans, because axial positions on adjacent carbons point to opposite sides of the ring
Cis, because both are axial
choices.why: Being axial doesn't make two hydrogens cis. Axial positions alternate faces, so adjacent axial hydrogens are on opposite sides.

choices.text: Cis, because they are on adjacent carbons
choices.why: Adjacency doesn't decide cis or trans; only the side of the ring does.

choices.text: Neither; cis and trans don't apply to axial hydrogens
choices.why: Any two ring hydrogens are cis if on the same side and trans if on opposite sides, axial or not.

explanation: Axial and equatorial positions alternate around each face: if carbons 1, 3, and 5 have axial hydrogens on top, carbons 2, 4, and 6 have axial hydrogens on the bottom. So the C1 and C2 axial hydrogens are on opposite sides, which makes them trans.

prompt: In chair cyclohexane, carbon 1 has its axial hydrogen on the top side. What is the relationship between the equatorial hydrogen on carbon 1 and the axial hydrogen on carbon 2?

choices.text: Cis, because both are on the bottom side of the ring
Trans, because one is axial and the other equatorial
choices.why: Axial versus equatorial doesn't decide cis or trans. Both of these hydrogens are on the bottom side, so they are cis.

choices.text: Trans, because they are on adjacent carbons
choices.why: Adjacency doesn't decide cis or trans; only the side of the ring does.

choices.text: Cis, because both are on the top side of the ring
choices.why: They are cis, but on the bottom: with C1's axial hydrogen on top, its equatorial hydrogen is on the bottom, as is C2's axial hydrogen.

explanation: With axial hydrogens on top at carbons 1, 3, and 5, carbons 1, 3, and 5 have equatorial hydrogens on the bottom, and carbons 2, 4, and 6 have axial hydrogens on the bottom. Two hydrogens on the same side of the ring are always cis, regardless of whether they're axial or equatorial.

prompt: How many distinct isomers of methylcyclohexane can be isolated at room temperature?
explanation: Even though chair cyclohexane has axial and equatorial positions, there is only one methylcyclohexane, because cyclohexane rings are conformationally mobile at room temperature. Different chair conformations readily interconvert by ring-flips, exchanging axial and equatorial positions.

prompt: Why is there only one bromocyclohexane, rather than separate axial and equatorial isomers?

choices.text: The chair conformations interconvert rapidly at room temperature by ring-flips, exchanging axial and equatorial positions
The bromine can only ever occupy an equatorial position
choices.why: Axial bromocyclohexane exists; it becomes equatorial bromocyclohexane after a ring-flip, and back again.

choices.text: Axial and equatorial positions are identical in energy and shape
choices.why: They are different kinds of positions. There's one compound because they interconvert, not because they're the same.

choices.text: Cyclohexane rings are rigid, so the bromine stays wherever it first bonds
choices.why: It's the reverse: cyclohexane rings are conformationally mobile at room temperature.

explanation: There is only one methylcyclohexane, one bromocyclohexane, one cyclohexanol, and so on, because cyclohexane rings are conformationally mobile at room temperature. Different chair conformations readily interconvert, exchanging axial and equatorial positions (Figure 4.6.4).

prompt: What happens to an axial bromine in bromocyclohexane when the ring flips?

choices.text: It becomes equatorial
It stays axial
choices.why: A ring-flip interconverts axial and equatorial positions: what is axial before becomes equatorial after.

choices.text: It moves to the neighboring carbon
choices.why: A ring-flip only changes the ring's conformation; no bonds break, so the bromine stays on the same carbon.

choices.text: It is lost, because a ring-flip breaks the C−Br bond
choices.why: A ring-flip is a change of conformation, not a reaction; the substituents all stay attached.

explanation: In a ring-flip, an axial substituent in one chair form becomes an equatorial substituent in the ring-flipped chair form and vice versa. Axial bromocyclohexane becomes equatorial bromocyclohexane (Figure 4.6.4).

prompt: How is a chair cyclohexane ring-flipped?

choices.text: The middle four carbons stay in place while the two end carbons fold in opposite directions
The whole molecule rotates 180° about the ring axis
choices.why: Rotating the whole molecule changes nothing about its shape; in a ring-flip the end carbons fold, which interconverts axial and equatorial positions.

choices.text: The two end carbons fold in the same direction
choices.why: The end carbons fold in opposite directions, one up and one down, to give the other chair.

choices.text: A C−C bond breaks and re-forms on the other side
choices.why: A ring-flip is a conformational change; no bonds break.

explanation: As shown in Figure 4.6.4, a chair cyclohexane can be ring-flipped by keeping the middle four carbon atoms in place while folding the two end carbons in opposite directions.

prompt: What is the approximate energy barrier to chair–chair interconversion in cyclohexane, in kJ/mol?
explanation: The energy barrier to chair–chair interconversion is only about 45 kJ/mol (10.8 kcal/mol), so the ring-flip is rapid at room temperature.

prompt: The ring-flip barrier in cyclohexane is only about 45 kJ/mol. What does this mean for what we observe at room temperature?

choices.text: Ring-flips are rapid, so we see what appears to be a single structure rather than distinct axial and equatorial isomers
Ring-flips are slow, so axial and equatorial isomers can be separated
choices.why: A barrier this low is easily crossed at room temperature, so the two chairs interconvert too fast to separate.

choices.text: Ring-flips never happen at room temperature
choices.why: The section describes the process as rapid at room temperature.

choices.text: The barrier locks each substituent in whichever position it starts in
choices.why: A barrier of 45 kJ/mol is low enough that the ring flips rapidly, so substituents keep exchanging axial and equatorial positions.

explanation: Since the energy barrier to chair–chair interconversion is only about 45 kJ/mol (10.8 kcal/mol), the process is rapid at room temperature and we see what appears to be a single structure rather than distinct axial and equatorial isomers.

prompt: In a chair conformation of 1,1-dichlorocyclohexane, how are the two chlorines on carbon 1 positioned?

choices.text: One is axial and the other equatorial
Both are axial
choices.why: Each carbon has only one axial position, so two groups on the same carbon can't both be axial.

choices.text: Both are equatorial
choices.why: Each carbon has only one equatorial position; the second group on carbon 1 must be axial.

choices.text: Both are axial in one chair and both equatorial after a ring-flip
choices.why: A ring-flip swaps them: the axial chlorine becomes equatorial and the equatorial one becomes axial, so there is still one of each.

explanation: Each carbon in chair cyclohexane has one axial and one equatorial position. Two groups on the same carbon must therefore occupy one of each: the one in the rough plane of the ring is equatorial, and the one directly above or below the ring is axial (Worked Example 4.6.1).

prompt: Looking at a chair drawing, how can you tell whether a substituent is axial or equatorial?

choices.text: A group directly above or below the ring is axial; a group in the rough plane of the ring is equatorial
A group above the ring is axial; a group below the ring is equatorial
choices.why: Axial groups point either up or down, parallel to the ring axis; equatorial groups stick out around the ring's edge.

choices.text: A group on the front (lower) bond is axial; a group on the back bond is equatorial
choices.why: Every carbon, front or back, has one axial and one equatorial position.

choices.text: A group in the rough plane of the ring is axial; a group directly above or below is equatorial
choices.why: That swaps the two. Axial positions are parallel to the ring axis, which runs straight up and down through the ring.

explanation: A substituent in the rough plane of the ring, around its equator, is equatorial; one pointing directly above or below the ring, parallel to the ring axis, is axial (Figure 4.6.1 and Worked Example 4.6.1).

prompt: A methyl group on cyclohexane starts in an equatorial position, and the ring then flips twice. Where is the methyl group now?

choices.text: Equatorial
Axial
choices.why: That is where it is after one ring-flip. The second flip exchanges the positions again, returning it to equatorial.

choices.text: On a different carbon
choices.why: Ring-flips change only the conformation; the methyl group stays on the same carbon.

choices.text: It depends on which direction the end carbons fold
choices.why: Every ring-flip exchanges axial and equatorial positions, so two flips always return the group to where it started.

explanation: Each ring-flip interconverts axial and equatorial positions: equatorial becomes axial after the first flip and equatorial again after the second (Figure 4.6.4).
